answer: Confidentiality (data stays private), Integrity (data stays accurate/unaltered), Availability (authorized users can access when needed).
Guarantees a party cannot deny an action — backed by digital signatures, audit logs and timestamps.
Verifies who you are, what you may do, and tracks/logs the activity performed.
"Never trust, always verify" — every user and device is continuously verified and given only the minimum access needed.
The component (firewall, endpoint agent, network device) in the Zero Trust data plane that enforces policies.
The Zero Trust control-plane component that evaluates policies and makes allow/deny decisions in real time.
Splitting the network into isolated zones so a compromise can not hop laterally.
Granting only the minimum permissions needed to perform a job or task.
Layered, independent security controls so failure of one layer does not compromise everything.
Stops incidents from occurring (firewalls, encryption, access-control mechanisms).
Identifies incidents that occur or have occurred (IDS, cameras, audit logs, FIM).
Restores or contains the impact of an incident (patch mgmt, system restore, quarantine).
Discourages attackers by visible defenses (warning banners, visible cameras).
An alternate control used when the primary control cannot be implemented (e.g. MFA instead of biometrics).
Guides behavior with policy, procedure, or regulation (security-policy sign-offs).
